newsitem.title: FINLAND: ANALYSTS SEE FINNISH ECONOMIC, EMU POLICY ON TRACK.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS SEE FINNISH ECONOMIC, EMU POLICY ON TRACK.

text.p: Finnish economic policy will not change and the government will not waver from its commitment to EMU, economists said after two government parties lost ground in municipal and European parliament elections on Sunday.
"I expect the government to stick with its policy," said Risto Murto, chief economist at brokerage Selin Finance.
"The implications (of the election results) for the government's economic policy are virtually zero," he said.
Dissent with the coalition's two leftist parties seemed to have caused a low turnout, keeping their defeats quite small.
"The government parties did not lose big, this bodes well for them in the 1999 general election," said Handelsbanken Markets Finland chief economist Carlo Erakallio.
"The outcome will increase significantly the government coalition's prospects of staying in office until 1999," he said.

He and Murto saw good prospects for the five-party left-right-green coalition, which took office in the spring of 1995 following a big victory for the Social Democrats after four years in opposition, to serve a full four-year term.
But the strong opposition to EMU highlighted by the election results may force political leaders to rethink their strategy.
"If trade unions turn openly anti-EMU, then the SDP might face trouble and this could slow down the process towards EMU," Erakallio said. "This is possible, but not a probable scenario."
"The potential implication for the EMU process is that the probability of Finland being in the first group to enter the single currency decreases, but very slightly," Selin's Murto said.

A research institute economic policy specialist said the government must consider seriously how to sell EMU to the public because "the opposition got quite an impressive victory, quite strong support for its anti-EMU stance".

"The question for them is now how to mobilise popular support for Finnish EMU membership ... to erase suspicions and uncertainties, to show that it is not a thing only for the ruling elite," he said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
It would be hard for Lipponen and the government to soften the stance on EMU, and retain credibility. "They have staked out their position so firmly in favour of EMU," he said.
Unlike the broad Finnish public, the government was aware how strong is the process among European leaders to bring about EMU, he said.
"It would be quite difficult for them (Finnish politicians) to suddenly distance themselves from this process and say that we are not interested," the research institute economist said.
Emphasising the commitment to EMU, the finance ministry on Monday briefed journalists on practical preparations in Finland for Economic and Monetary Union in 1999.

"The political drive towards EMU is very, very strong," a senior finance ministry official told reporters. He said he was referring to Europe in general, but his message echoed Lipponen on Sunday: "The EMU train has left and the only alternative for the government is to act as if EMU will take off in 1999."

On Monday, Finland's financial markets expressed confidence in the coalition led by fiscal austerity hawks Lipponen and Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto, the leader of the Conservative Party, which market analysts noted was among Sunday's winners.
Bond yields edged lower and the 10-year yield gap over German Bunds narrowed one basis point to 48. The markka was stable around 2.99 per German mark.
With the elections past, "one uncertainty factor is now out of the way", Erakallio at Handelsbanken said. "This will have a stabilising effect on the markets," he added.
